extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP litigators, and patent office/PTAB practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: A practitioner-oriented year-in-review summarizing 2024 Federal Circuit, PTAB, and Supreme Court (none this year) decisions across major patent-law topics (§101 subject matter, anticipation/obviousness/prior art, enablement/written description, IPR practice, venue/jurisdiction, claim construction, infringement/damages, design patents, interferences, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step §101 framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the two-step Alice/Mayo analysis: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea (or other ineligible concept); (2) if so, determine whether the claims recite an ‘inventive concept’ that transforms the abstract idea into patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to whether claims recite a specific technological solution or merely result-oriented, functional language. Generic computer components performing conventional tasks typically do not supply an inventive concept. Claims that improve computer functionality or recite specific means or methods that solve a technical problem may be eligible. Case examples: Chewy (targeted advertising found abstract), AI Visualize (data retrieval/manipulation/display at high level of generality found abstract), Contour (claims found eligible where they recited a specific dual-recording wireless camera solution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-claim practice in §101 analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may evaluate a single representative claim (or small group) for eligibility when claims are 'substantially similar and linked to the same' ineligible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating claims as representative is proper when parties agree or the patent owner does not present meaningful arguments distinguishing other claims; if a patent owner makes a non-frivolous argument that the representative claim does not fairly represent other claims, the challenger bears the burden to prove otherwise. (Mobile Acuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 as an affirmative defense at pleading stage
rubrics_metrics.description: A §101 challenge is an affirmative defense that can be evaluated at the pleading stage when the defense 'clearly appears on the face of the pleadings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent(s) are attached to the complaint, courts may consider their content on a Rule 12 motion and dismiss where patent-ineligible subject matter plainly appears from the patent. (Mobile Acuity; district courts applying Ninth Circuit law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/result-oriented claim language signals abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims drafted using largely result-focused, functional language are strong indicators of an abstract idea and are frequently found ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts cite result-oriented phrasing and omission of how steps are performed as reasons to find abstractness; claiming goals such as 'achieving X' without specific technical means often fails Alice step two. (Beteiro, AI Visualize, Mobile Acuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional components and conventional steps do not supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of generic databases, servers, conventional offline/batch processing, GPS in phones, templates, or automation of human tasks ordinarily will not provide the 'inventive concept' required at Alice step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely automate abstract ideas using well-understood, routine, conventional computer components or that claim improved speed/efficiency without novel technical means are typically ineligible. (Chewy, Broadband, Beteiro, Contour contrast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that claims show how a technical problem is solved
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible, claims that involve computer/technical subject matter should recite how the claimed elements effect the solution to the technological problem, not merely state the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether the specification and claim limitations disclose details of the purported technical solution; mere specification descriptions without claim limitations specifying the details often fail to show an inventive concept. (AI Visualize, Mobile Acuity, Contour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed-publication prior art standard (accessibility/dissemination)
rubrics_metrics.description: A document can be a 'printed publication' prior art if it was disseminated or otherwise accessible to the interested public, even if distribution was limited, depending on context and intent of dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution to a limited set with confidentiality restrictions may or may not be a publication; courts distinguish cases like Cordis (academic monographs to a few colleagues) from commercial manuals created for dissemination to customers and obtainable upon purchase/request, which can be prior art. (Weber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private sale as prior art and limits of post-AIA §102(b) safe harbor
rubrics_metrics.description: A private sale of an invention can be invalidating prior art (on-sale bar) but may not invoke the post-AIA §102(b) safe harbor against later disclosures by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent cases (Allergan and Sanho referenced) hold private sales can be prior art but do not automatically create a safe-harbor situation under post-AIA §102(b); practitioners should analyze on-sale facts and applicable statutory safe-harbors carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial sales or offers for sale can create prior-art bars (on-sale) that invalidate claims if the invention was on sale before the critical date under applicable law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts continue to scrutinize pre-critical-date sales, private deals, and related activities; the analysis intersects with printed-publication and §102 rules (see introduction and on-sale cases referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness: analogous art and motivation to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish obviousness, a challenger must show a skilled artisan would have been motivated to combine prior art references and that the references are analogous art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB findings of motivation to combine can be supported by expert testimony and factual record (evidence of why a skilled artisan would look to a particular reference or method). The Federal Circuit will defer to substantial evidence on these factual determinations. (LG/CyWee example; ZyXEL v. UNMRI discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-patenting / 'patentably distinct' meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a later patent or application cannot be asserted if they are not 'patentably distinct' from claims finally refused or canceled in an IPR under 37 C.F.R. § 42.73(d)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO intended 'patentably distinct' to carry its specialized patent-law meaning (as used in obviousness-type double patenting). The rule prevents obtaining claims in any patent that are not patentably distinct from previously canceled/refused claims. (Softview).

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB motion-to-amend requirements and Motion-to-Amend Pilot Program
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions to amend should contain written-description support for substitute claims (37 C.F.R. § 42.121(b)), but the Motion-to-Amend Pilot permits the patent owner to file replies that may supply missing written-description evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTAB may accept evidence submitted with a reply under the Pilot Program to correct or supplement an initial motion to amend; appellate courts will consider whether any procedural error was harmless (i.e., no prejudice). (ZyXEL v. UNMRI).

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB timing rules for objections to evidence and motions to exclude expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to evidence must be timely under PTAB rules: generally within 10 business days of institution of trial for certain objections (37 C.F.R. § 42.64(b)(1)), and objections to evidence presented during trial must be filed within five business days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to object within the prescribed windows can result in denial of exclusion motions as untimely; challenges to expert testimony often go to weight/credibility rather than admissibility if timely raised. (ZyXEL v. UNMRI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture and rehearing practice in PTAB appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a request for rehearing under 37 C.F.R. § 42.71(d) is optional; failure to include an argument in a rehearing request does not automatically forfeit the right to appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, a party may forfeit arguments it never presented to the Board because the appellate court is deprived of the Board’s informed consideration. Preservation before the Board remains important to avoid forfeiture. (Voice Tec v. Unified Patents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel effect of IPR final decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims or positions rejected in an IPR can have estoppel consequences in later PTO proceedings and limit a patent owner from obtaining claims not patentably distinct from those finally refused or canceled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 42.73(d)(3) prohibits actions inconsistent with an adverse IPR judgment; the Board may rely on this regulation to refuse claims deemed not patentably distinct. (Softview).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-patent obviousness standard (Rosen-Durling overruled)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit overruled the rigid Rosen-Durling two-part test for design-patent obviousness and held that obviousness for designs should be analyzed under the Graham/KSR flexible framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Graham factors and KSR principles (a flexible, obviousness-focused inquiry) to design patents rather than requiring a Rosen 'Rosen reference' and Durling-limited secondary-reference application. (LKQ v. GM en banc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference §135(b)(1) time-bar and 'same or substantially the same subject matter' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 135(b)(1) bars later-filed application claims that are the same as or for the same (or substantially the same) subject matter as a claim of an issued patent if not made prior to one year from the patent grant; this is a statute of repose with limited exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply a comparison (two-way test) to determine whether pre-critical-date claims provide support for later claims; material differences (e.g., presence/absence of a limitation like 'free of containment material') can render a claim time-barred. There is an exception where the applicant was 'already claiming substantially the same invention' during the critical period. (Speck v. Bates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent’s specification must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention by describing the invention with sufficient detail to show the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere conclusory allegations or generic descriptions without specifics about how limitations are achieved do not satisfy written description; substitute claims in PTAB motions must be supported by written-description evidence (see Motion to Amend discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be sufficiently definite so that a person of ordinary skill can determine the scope of the claims with reasonable certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Year-in-Review includes a dedicated section on indefiniteness (IV.A) addressing the standard and cases; patentees should ensure claim terms are defined or used in a way that avoids uncertainty (heading present; cases not shown in excerpt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct / unclean hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequitable conduct defenses require proof of material misrepresentation/omission to the PTO and intent to deceive; courts evaluate whether conduct warrants equitable relief (forfeiture of patent rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review contains a section on unclean hands and inequitable conduct (V) summarizing relevant 2024 decisions; practitioners should document reasonable prosecution conduct and disclosures to avoid malpractice/exclusion risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents and inducement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving infringement under the doctrine of equivalents remains subject to a high evidentiary bar; inducement analyses consider labels and other contextual factors to determine whether inducement occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit reaffirmed a high bar for doctrine-of-equivalents claims and continued to explore what external indicia (e.g., skinny labels) can be considered in inducement assessments. Practitioners should craft infringement theories with clear nexus to claim elements and evidence of intent where inducement is alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages standards: EMV, reasonable royalties, foreign conduct considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages decisions in 2024 addressed issues such as foreign conduct, allocation of damages, reasonable-royalty calculations, and the entire-market-value (EMV) rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts continue to require a clear nexus between the patented feature and the accused product's value for EMV relief and scrutinize expert testimony on royalty bases and apportionment. The Year-in-Review summarizes Federal Circuit guidance on these damage topics (section IX and cases noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction guidance: specification limits vs non-limiting embodiments; printed-matter doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: When construing claims, courts assess whether the specification limits claim scope to the 'present invention' or whether preferred embodiments are non-limiting; printed-matter doctrine issues also arise in claim interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document contains a section (VIII) addressing specification-limiting issues and the printed-matter doctrine; patentees should avoid language that unintentionally limits claims and ensure claim scope is supported by specification disclosure.
